title: Prosecutor v. Mile Mrkšić — killing of prisoners of war from Vukovar hospital
question: Was the commander of the forces in control of the area criminally responsible for the killing of prisoners of war taken from a hospital after the surrender of Croatian forces?
facts: Croatian forces in the Vukovar area capitulated on 18 November 1991. An agreement provided for wounded or sick patients fit to travel to be evacuated to Croatia, with the hospital under ICRC protection and the evacuation monitored by the European Community Monitoring Mission. On 19 November, the JNA entered Vukovar hospital; military police of the Guards Motorised Brigade took over security. More than 200 men, and two women, who were or were believed to have been involved in Croatian forces were taken from the hospital on 20 November. The initial plan was to transport the men under JNA guard to the prisoner-of-war facility at Sremska Mitrovica, where they could later be exchanged for Serb prisoners held by Croatian authorities. At the JNA barracks, local Territorial Defence and paramilitary forces threatened and verbally abused the men; JNA military police removed those forces from the compound. The prisoners were subsequently taken to a hangar at Ovčara. JNA military police guarded them there, but Territorial Defence and paramilitary forces had access to them at times, and the guards' efforts were inconsistent. Members of those forces severely beat prisoners at the hangar. Some senior JNA officers visited and tried to improve the military police response, with effects that were ineffective or temporary. Between 2000 and 2100 hours, an order from the command of Operational Group South directed the JNA military police guarding the prisoners to withdraw. The prisoners were then in the custody of the Vukovar Territorial Defence. Territorial Defence and paramilitary forces took prisoners in small groups to an isolated location and shot them. At least 200 persons died at Ovčara on 20 and 21 November 1991, in almost all cases from gunshot wounds; 194 of the persons named in the indictment were among those killed. The commander of Operational Group South had earlier ordered that the prisoners be taken to Sremska Mitrovica. Local Territorial Defence and paramilitary forces were hostile to members of the Croatian forces. A number of JNA officers reported to the commander the conduct of those forces at the JNA barracks and at Ovčara, and he was informed of killings at Velepromet the preceding day. The local Serb government opposed the transfer of prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica, and its wishes appear to have been a significant factor in the commander's decision concerning their custody.
holding: In its Trial Judgment of 27 September 2007, the ICTY Trial Chamber found Mile Mrkšić guilty under Article 7(1) for aiding and abetting murder, torture, and cruel treatment, as violations of the laws or customs of war under Article 3. The crimes-against-humanity counts were dismissed for all three accused because the victims were not civilians for the purposes of Article 5. The three accused were treated differently: Miroslav Radić was acquitted on all counts; Mrkšić was convicted of murder, torture, and cruel treatment; and Veselin Šljivančanin was convicted of torture only and acquitted on the other counts. The Chamber imposed a single sentence of 20 years' imprisonment on Mrkšić.
key_reasoning: The commander knew of the high risk of serious violence and death to the prisoners from the Territorial Defence and paramilitary forces.
He ordered the withdrawal of the JNA military police guarding the prisoners, after which those forces had unrestricted access to them.
It was not established that the commander ordered the Territorial Defence and paramilitary forces to commit the crimes; his responsibility was as an aider and abettor.
